utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. May we have the appearances for today, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. On behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor, I'm Tom Hannis, along with Selma Sakic, and Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence this afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic, Aleksandar Aleksic, and Ms. Marie Pineaud. For the record, our client, Mr. Zupljanin, is not present today and I hope that his waiver will be filed in the usual manner in due course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The next witness is ST-219. We filed last week, on Thursday, I believe, an urgent request for protective measures. However, I think Your Honours may want to hear directly from the witness before you make your final decision about it. And also, related to the documents I proposed to use with this witness, there is one, at tab 11. It's Exhibit P630. Early this morning we received a revised English translation of that document. While preparing for this witness and looking at it, it appeared to me that there were some problems with the previous translation that had been in e-court. I requested the revised translation. That's been received. I think it's uploaded in e-court and we'd like leave of the Court to substitute that English translation for the one that is currently in e-court. It has no bearing on the original B/C/S of which there is a hard copy in the field office to be used by the witness. But for our purposes, if I indeed use it today, it would be good to have the revised version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Dealing with the second matter first. Does the Defence have any observations about the application to substitute --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we do not oppose the -- the application made by my learned friend Mr. Hannis; however, we would like to be reminded of the reference on the -- on the -- on the translation where the problem was before, so that we can compare it now before we can finally say that we don't have any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There wasn't a single word. It was very much a matter of grammar and phrasing. It was almost unintelligible in parts and I think it's clear now. I couldn't point you to a specific sentence or paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But it has been done by CLSS, the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The revised translation, I don't know. It was done so quickly, I suspect it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, then we do object.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As a practical matter. I think it was probably done in-house. But it is certainly more intelligible than the previous translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand the reason, but I think the previous translation was done by the translation unit of the Office of the Prosecutor and that caused the problem. And it was my understanding that once its is resent for translation it should be CLSS. That is our position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could we approach it this way. I assume that the Defence has no objection on principle to the substitution because everybody is interested in the accuracy of the material that is provided. The -- that we -- that the Chamber takes no action on the application for substitution until the Defences has satisfied themselves that they have not inadvertently created any new problems. Would that be the more practical approach?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Definitely, Your Honours. I appreciate your suggestion and that is how -- we don't -- we do not objection to the principle. That is for sure. We just need to be given some time to review the translation in order that -- that we -- we can check whether it corresponds to the original, in our opinion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And I suppose that, Mr. Pantelic, you echo Mr. Zecevic's position?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Are you on board with this, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. Appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the Chamber makes the usual inquiries directly of the witness, I seem to recall that there had been no response as such to the application for protective measures. Is that the ... What is the Defence's position?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We take no position at this point, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We take no position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Can the Court Officer hear me? Let's make sure, first of all, that the technical transmission is working.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Hear you fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And the witness is present with you, I take it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honours. The witness is present with me in the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Could you place him so that can he be seen by the camera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, until we resolve the matter [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honours [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... request because it includes a request for image distortion. I guess we need to go into private session or in some manner to avoid revealing his face, if that's the ultimate decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I was trying to think through what the electronic equivalent is to what we would have done in terms of lowering the blinds and whatnot. And ... I'm advised that it would be sufficient for us to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in private session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, I would, first of all, invite you to read the solemn declaration which the Court Officer has now placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I would, first of all, point out to you that that solemn declaration that you have just made imposes upon you an obligation to give truthful testimony to this Tribunal, and the penalty for failing to do so is the -- are the penalties which this Tribunal, by its constituent Statute, are able to impose for perjury on person who is give untruthful or misleading testimony. We have before us, before your testimony is heard an application filed by the Prosecution at your request, at your insistence, requesting certain protective measures. I would, first of all, explain that ordinarily the testimony is received by the Tribunal in open session that is, even when a witness is testifying via videolink such as you are. And the reason for this is, that, being a criminal Tribunal, it is imperative that the public, especially in the region of the former -- the countries that comprise the former Yugoslavia, have confidence in the integrity of the proceedings and that everyone who comes before the Tribunal has a public trial, that is, a trial to which members of the public has access. Notwithstanding that principle, it is recognised and has been recognised over the life of the Tribunal that, where there are good and valid reasons for doing so, witnesses may be allowed certain protective measures in the wider interests of justice so that, on the one hand, the Tribunal has the benefit of the best evidence that it can obtain; and, on the other hand, that witnesses or their family members are not -- are not unnecessarily put at risk. And it is for that reason that the Tribunal is empowered in exceptional circumstances to permit to a witness who has made his concerns known to the side calling him that there are reasons why certain protective measures should be employed. So, could you, first of all, tell us what your concerns are; and, secondly, what measures you are seeking that would allay your concerns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation], first of all, I'm a family man. I have two children. And it's because of my children, because I don't want them to have problems in the near or further future because I'm appearing as a witness. As far as I'm personally concerned, all my neighbours know who I was and, to some extent, the people in the organisation where I work, and that's the Ministry of Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, since people were looking for me, mentioning my name. But as far as I myself am concerned, I wouldn't have sought protective measures. But if that is not possible, we can go into open session and there should be no problems. That's what I would have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: There is an question that I'm direct to go counsel for the Prosecution: Mr. Hannis, the -- I -- I don't have your motion in front of me, but the -- was this the witness in respect of whom there was the -- it was represented that the name was such that -- would you like to ask the witness a question directly related to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour. Examination on Protective Measures by Mr. Hannis:

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. I want to ask you about the information --

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to ask you about the information that I provided to the Court concerning your request for protective measures. And in that motion we indicated a couple of things. You had some concerns for your family possibly being harassed, if it were learned that you had testified here at the Tribunal. And one of the reasons you indicated was that your name, Ranko Vukovic, is a rather common name in the territory, that you had already been harassed once at least because some non-Serb persons thought you were a Ranko Vukovic from Foca who allegedly had committed some crimes against non-Serbs during the war. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It happened at the ministry, because I work at the Ministry of Defence, and since there is one Ranko Vukovic who was sentenced to 12 and a half years imprisonment by the court, and I was born in Foca in 1952. So some individuals, one Suad Roko who is a religious officer, said to me, Oh, so you're the Ranko. And I said, There are many Rankos and where I live currently there is about a dozen Ranko Vukovics within a circle of about 110 kilometres. And the second thing, there was police director by the name of Ranko Vukovic in the Republika Srpska who had his personal ID taken away from him and his freedom of movement was limited. I believe these measures were lifted recently. But I'm not that Ranko Vukovic either. I'm a man who respects everybody irrespective of the colour of their skin, their name, their ethnic affiliation and their religion. I am this Ranko Vukovic. I believe that this is enough. You're right, Mr. Hannis, and when we spoke at Nedzarici in Sarajevo, you understood me correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would indicate that reference to that second Ranko Vukovic was an individual suspected of having some association with a network protected Mr. Karadzic when he was a fugitive, and his reference to his ID and limitation on movement related to actions taken by the UN High Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Vukovic? That's the second one you were talking about.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And finally, Your Honours, one last thing. Mr. Vukovic, in our motion, we also indicated that you had some concerns about possible harassment or retaliation against your family members by Serb extremists simply by the fact that you were testifying at the Tribunal in a case where the accused are Serbs. Is that correct? Was that -- is that a concern you have?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: I told you that I couldn't testify about some things of which I have no knowledge. I cannot confirm some things for the OTP. And possibly for that reason, some people who belonged to my ethnic group could be induced to think that I stated some things that weren't true. That's why I said that. But I also said that my daughter who has a diploma in English could come to work for the joint institutions in Sarajevo. And for that reason, my child could face some problems caused by the Bosniak side or another side, because I'm her father. Although I state with full responsibility that I haven't had any problems with the law, that I have a clean slate and clean hands, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vukovic. I don't have any further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Do counsel for the Defence have any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't need to question the witness, but, Your Honours, because I don't want to use up the time. We know for a fact that witness testified for the Defence in two previous cases or was supposed to testify for Defence -- gave the statements for -- for the Defence in Krajisnik and Karadzic. None of the reasons which were stated over -- in -- in -- in our friend's motion has been confirmed by -- by the witness basically. I -- I probably missed something, but I don't see how -- how the fact that some other people have the same name and the surname is relevant for any of this, because the witness will not be changing his name. That's for sure. So the problems with the same name and other persons having the same name will persist whether he testifies publicly or testifies under the protective measures, so I don't see how is that relevant for this. And in my opinion, there is -- according to the witness there is -- there is no -- there was no threats, he's just -- he's just having some concerns which -- which have no basis for -- whatsoever at this point in time in the -- or -- or any actual events. Therefore, saying all this, we -- we do oppose now to the -- to -- to granting the protective measures. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, although this witness is not related to our client, I mean, generally but as a matter of principle we support position of Stanisic Defence with that regard. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I may, I'm not trying to continue to argue the motion, just to clarify a couple of points. Mr. Zecevic said that this witness testified before. To my knowledge, he has not testified before at this Tribunal. He did give a one-page witness statement apparently to the Krajisnik Defence but he was not called as a witness in that case, and I think he may have been listed as a potential witness for Mr. Karadzic's Defence but he has not testified in that case yet. And the reason we're referring to his name is, that relates to the request for a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I heard you say that you are -- that you -- you -- you're currently employed in the Ministry of Defence. Is that Republika Srpska Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It's the Ministry of Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Because the federal Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of Defence of the RS have been abolished, and they were integrated into one state level Ministry of Defence, for which I work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And you're of Serb ethnicity; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And in 1992, you -- for -- you worked for the Ministry of Defence as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Having heard the witness -- having heard the witness and having considered the submissions and representations made by counsel on both sides, the decision of the Trial Chamber is that the witness may be afforded a pseudonym. That is the limit of the protective measures that we consider necessary in the circumstances of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We've asked for him to have the pseudonym ST-219. He does have a pseudonym sheet down there, I guess. I don't know how you want to deal with that in this videolink context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, the Court Officer has just passed to you a pseudonym sheet. If you are satisfied that that correctly states your name and your date of birth, please sign it and pass it back to him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before we move into open session, I would remind the parties and, indeed, ourselves, that having regard to the pseudonym, which the witness has been granted to avoid mentioning his name, and, of course, if the -- he would be other -- if there is any answer which would compromise the pseudonym then, of course, we would revert to private session. So we move into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you before I invite counsel for the Prosecution who has called you, to begin his questions, the -- continuing with the preliminary questions that the Chamber would have of you, the -- you have never testified before this Tribunal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Have you testified before a court in any of the countries in the former Yugoslavia, in terms of the events that -- that -- that arose out of the -- 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- thank you - procedure is that the side calling you would begin, and the -- then counsel for each of the accused has a right to ask you questions arising out of the questions which the Prosecution has asked. The Prosecution then has a right to re-examine and at that stage or indeed at any earlier stage the Bench may have questions for you. It is expected that the Prosecution would spent an hour and a half with you and counsel for accused Stanisic has indicated that they may be with you for as long as five hours, but I believe that that has been since amended and it would not be nearly as long as -- did I see something about 30 minutes and some.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I said that we are going to be considerably shorter with the cross-examination and it's probably going to be a one hour and a half or one session maybe, in that range. I informed my learned friend from the Office of the Prosecutor over the weekend about that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. You would have heard the exchange between the Bench and Mr. Zecevic who appears for the accused Stanisic. He has indicated that he too would be with you for about an hour and a half, and counsel for the accused Zupljanin, if they have any questions at all, would not exceed an hour. The Court day is -- begins --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If it is an afternoon session such as this is, it starts at 2.15 an ends at 7.00 and the reason for the court day being divided as it is is that that the limited court facilities have to be shared with other trials. We are scheduled to resume your testimony which, having regard to the time indications I have given, are unlikely to be completed by the time we rise at 7.00 this evening. And it is due to continue tomorrow by the time we take -- we rise I would indicate whether it would be in the morning or in the afternoon. Now, within those breaks, within those time-limits of 2.15 to 7.00 p.m., or if it is a morning session from 9.00 to 1.45, there are breaks every 90 minutes for two reasons. One, is that the tapes which are used to record the proceedings have to be changed at 90-minute intervals and that also allows witnesses to -- witnesses, counsel, the Bench themselves, to take a break. Now, if the -- during any of the 20-minute breaks that we have before between the sessions, you find it necessary that we take a break we will, of course, accommodate you, and with that, I would invite Mr. Hannis to begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. One more procedural matter. I think we need to give the pseudonym sheet an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And the Court Officer did hand me the reminder and I still forgot. I'm sorry. The pseudonym sheet should be given -- admitted under seal and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the pseudonym sheet for ST-219 shall be admitted as P01722, under seal. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I confirm we are still in open session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, then I think I need to go briefly into private session just for some personal details that might reveal his identity in terms of background. If I may.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, before the war began in 1992, in 1991, can you tell us where you were working and what position you held.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: In 1991, I worked in the Ministry of Defence, in the Secretariat for National Defence in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what position did you hold there?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: I was an operative at the alarming and reporting centre in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you have any managerial or supervisory position?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: I attended a school for chiefs of the centre, in Zemen [phoen], and I completed that school. And in that period, I was chief of the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in April, early April of 1992, after the war began in Bosnia, did your municipal centre for alarming and reporting get converted to being a republic centre?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Before the war, in the former Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the former Yugoslavia, the centre was on a municipal level and it was subordinated to the town centre for monitoring and information of the town of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And after the war, what became of your centre? Did it assume a new -- a new status?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: After the war, this centre continued to function as a regional centre for monitoring information and cryptographic data protection in Pale. However, up to 1998 in -- during the period of the war, this is what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during the period of war, was your centre in Pale the republic centre for communications and cryptodatic protection, for the entire Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes. Between 1992 and 1998, the communications and cryptographic data protection centre in Pale was on the level of the republic for the entire Republika Srpska. As well as for the service for monitoring and information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we can go back into open session for the time being.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, if I ask a question to which you think the answer might reveal your name, and you have a concern about that, to please let us know that you might wish to answer that in private session. Would you please?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: That's fine. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Prior to the war breaking out in April of 1992, as I understand it, there were a system of alarming and reporting centres throughout the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the job of these centres was, among other things, to alert the authorities and alert and inform the population about natural disasters or man-made disasters or the threat of armed invasion, things like that?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: After April 1992, when the conflict began and there was a republic centre for communications in Pale, what other task did that centre perform rather than simply informing and alerting? What was its role concerning communications for the republic?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: In April, when the centre started working as a republic centre of communications and cryptographic data protection and monitoring and information in Pale, it was our obligation to monitor the situation in the territory, to monitor the situation in the air and on water and to discover as early as possible all dangers that might threaten the civilian population, army units or institutions, and other structures of the socio-political community. As for communications we worked on cryptographic data protection of written information. However, at the beginning of this unfortunate period of the war in early April, there were a lot of problems in the functioning of the communications systems, as well as in establishing visual monitoring in the field because of the combat operations and because of the low number of people who had the training to be distributed in these centres. In the first months of the war, April and May, until about June, we didn't have a developed system to protect military data. We didn't have a developed code so that we could protect information. We were able to communicate with the town centre in Sarajevo throughout the month of April, and even during part of May, until we encountered certain problems so we lost this communication. It was cut off. That's what circumstances were like. We had all kinds of communication with the socio-political communities and with the organs of the authorities which were located in Pale, as well as with other institutions. And due to a lack of men, we had the role of republic centre, regional centre and municipal centre, of the cryptographic data protection system and of monitoring and information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In addition to that system in the Ministry of Defence, in 1992, what were the other primary communications networks or systems in the Republika Srpska? Did the VRS have its own?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes. The armed forces have their own communications system. The Ministry of Interior had its own communication system, independent of the army, and independent of the communications of the socio-political community. And the Ministry of Defence had its own communication systems, and these communication system were independent of each other and they were able to function independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned the communications of the socio-political community. Was that something that was served by the Ministry of Defence's system, or is that a fourth system, in addition to Ministry of Defence, Ministry of Interior, and the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: That was within the centres of the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the Ministry of Defence, who -- who was the primary customer, if you will, in terms of communication? For what primary individuals or institutions or organs did the Ministry of Defence furnish communications in 1992? Apart from the Ministry of Defence itself.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: The primary purpose and the function of the republic centre and of the other centres that were linked based on the chain of command to the republic centre of the Ministry of Defence was to service the organs of the authorities, the civilian structures of the authorities, from the lower level to the very highest level. The Presidency, the government, ministries of all organs in the government, and the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At the highest level, did that include the assembly for the Serb people, or the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes. Because the Assembly of Republika Srpska was a civilian organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In the communications centre, the republic communications centre in Pale in 1992, can you tell the Judges what kinds of communication equipment there was?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: We had three departments. We had a radio department; a telephone department; and a cryptographic data protection department.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I take it from that description, then, you had phone, telephones; correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Radios, I understand from other witnesses that included both short wave and ultra short wave?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes. We had short-wave radios, and we had ultra short-wave radios.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Fax machines?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: We had fax machines where the telephone and teleprinting service was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I take it from that answer you also had teletype machines or teleprinter in your centre.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes. We had a teleprinter in the telegraph service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you have radio relay capability in that centre?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes. We had radio relay communications as well. Wire communications, radio relay communications, and radio communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I take it, if none of that worked, you also had human couriers for purposes of delivering communications?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes, there were couriers as well. There was a developed courier system of communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to have you take a look at an exhibit. This is tab 3 in the binder that you have down there. It's Exhibit 1D170. This is a document you will have seen before dated the 16th of April, 1992. Do you remember seeing this document before, sir?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes. I saw the document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me go into private session for --

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: I saw it perhaps 20 days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me go into private session for one or two question, if I may.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in private session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sir, if you would look, it's at the bottom, near the bottom of the second page in your B/C/S and it's the bottom of page 2 in English. Under the name of the minister, Bogdan Subotic, there's a part that in my English translation says, "Transmitted by Vukovic on 16 April 1992 at 1006." Is that you?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes, that is me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What is this in terms of what kind of document it is. Is this a telegram or a teletype, can you tell me, please?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Since we did not have a system of cryptographic data protection on 16 April this document was teletyped and sent through open communication means. And you can see the number of our teleprinter service at Pale, which is 41505 and you also see the number of the receiving service, 45100. This telegram was sent by teleprinter. This teleprinter connection was between Pale and Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going go back into open session and when we are in open session I'll ask you some further questions about this document and ask you not give any answer that would indicate that you were the sender of it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on the first page of this document, can you tell us what the 0959 at the top refers to? Is that the time that this message would have been started to be sent?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There is a reference number --

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: That's the time when ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Please finish.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: At that time, the contact was established between the two teleprinter services.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And the reference number, 1-92, does that indicate that this is the first message that's been sent by the new Ministry of National Defence in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Judging by the document, that should have been the first telegram that was ever sent on the 16th of April, 1992; hence the number 1/92.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if could you go to the second page, at the bottom where there's a typed signature for the National Defence minister, Mr. Subotic, there's a "Transmitted By," on such a date at 1006, and then it says: "Received" by a certain individual for Banja Luka. In terms of how the teletype works can you explain to me when and how the name of the recipient gets on the document? If, for example, I were sitting in Pale typing this document into the teleprinter to be sent from Pale to Banja Luka, who types in that name at the end where it says: "Received." Is that done in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes, that is added in Banja Luka. The operative who received the telegram he also signed the receipt of the telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you say "signed it," you mean signed it electronically by typing in his name?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: This telegram could have been sent manually or it could also have been sent by means of perforated band. On the end of the sending of either a telegram or any other document the operative who received it, signed the document off to confirm that he, indeed, received it at a certain time. And can you see it in the stamp at the end of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That was my next question. The stamp at the end of the document, can you tell us where that's from and when and where it would have been put on this document? Is it a stamp at Pale or a stamp at Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: When you look at the stamp, you can see that the document was received under number 440/800 on the 16th of April 1992, at 1010 hours than it was received by teleprinter. I can't read the signature. It's illegible. I wouldn't be able to tell you who received the telegram, whether it was Jerko Batinar, whether he was the one who put his signature in the stamp, I don't know. There should be a log-book for all the outgoing telegrams, as well as log-book of all the incoming telegrams in Banja Luka where all the received telegrams are recorded. I can't really tell you that that was that. I would have to consult the log-books which I don't have. If you could show me one of those log-books, I would be able to complete my answer. I would be able to tell you who signed the stamp, whether it was Jerko Batinar or somebody else. The signature itself is not legible enough for me to tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. One more thing before we leave this document. At the top of the first page, there is what appears to be a fax header. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what does that indicate to you? Was this actual hard copy of this teletype message then also faxed after it was received, or can you say?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: The top of the document, you can see that the memorandum was in the centre in Banja Luka and as far as I can remember, the number indicated on the document was the number of the fax in the Banja Luka centre. I can't tell you whether the operative faxed this document to somebody else. I don't know that. I'm not able to see it from the document without the log-book. If I saw the log-book I would be able to tell you who the document was sent to. Since Banja Luka was a regional centre at the time, and this document applied to all Serbian municipalities, I suppose that he did fax the document to the municipalities in the Krajina region.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank --

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: And that's what I can conclude, based on just looking at the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have all the log-books I would like to have to show you, and I don't have all the time to show you everything. One last thing: There is a stamp on the first page in the upper right-hand corner. Can you tell us what that is, where it's from?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: And judging by the inscription, I can see that the stamp had something to do with the Krajina region.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If you could next take a look at the document that's behind tab 5 in your binder. This is Exhibit P467. This is a document that's dated the 4th of May, 1992. And if you would look at the second page, you'll see the name of the sender as being a Colonel Miodrag Sajic of the Regional Secretariat for NO. Can you tell me what NO stands for in this context?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: The Regional Secretariat for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you know Colonel Sajic?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know how many Regional Centres of National Defence there were in May of 1992 in the Republika Srpska, or the Serb Republic of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: After such a long time, I can only try to recall how many there were. But I'm not sure that I will be able to give you the exact number. You know, I have already told you that had a car accident. I had a retrograde and antegrade amnesia. It is possible that I will not be able to remember. I forgot a lot of things. There was a regional Secretariat for National Defence in Banja Luka. There was also one in Bijeljina. There was regional Secretariat for National Defence in Trebinje. There was another one at Pale, in the then-Serbian Sarajevo. And there was also Regional Secretariat in Doboj, I think. This is as much as I can recall after such a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And as I understand it, the MOD republic communications centre had links with all of those regional centres at this time; correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: There were certain periods of time where -- when there were connections but those connections were rather impaired, so contacts were not so easy to establish. There were very frequent outages of electricity, there were also works in the territory of the armed forces or some groups, telephone cables were damaged so it was not so easy to establish communication at all times. Therefore, there were periods when we had to use some other means in order to be able to communicate tasks to each other. We were successful [as interpreted] all the time. We had to use open communications means, even radio communications at times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you see from the first paragraph in this document it makes reference to that 16 April decision of Minister Subotic that we looked at before; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I'm looking at the document I can see that it is the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I need to mention in transcript, 26, 20, I believe the witness said, "We were not successful all the time." And it was recorded as, "We were successful."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sure that will be caught when the transcript is reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm sorry, did I understand your answer, Witness, that this document is referring to that 16 April dispatch number 1-92 from the minister of defence?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: From the preamble of this decision that I have before me, I can see that the document was number 1-92 dated 16 April 1992. However, after such a long time, without consulting the log-book of outgoing and incoming telegrams, I cannot say anything for certain. This is not the original of the document. Therefore, I wouldn't be able to tell you whether this document corresponds to the original document. This is a photocopy; that's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: It's not an original.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that. But 1-92 from the Ministry of Defence, is that one that we looked at earlier, announcing mobilisation and the declaration of an imminent threat of war; correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: It is possible. However, after such a long time --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: I cannot interpret the minister's decision or the decision of any other official, for that matter --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: -- anybody who used the services of our centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me show you the next tab. Tab 6. This is Exhibit P555. This is also dated the 4th of May, 1992. And looking at the format, can you tell me what kind of document this is? Would this have been sent by teletype or teleprinter? Can you say?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: It was probably sent as a teletype message. This is a document that was sent by a Siemens teleprinter machine. However, I have not seen this decision before. And the signature is of the centre chief, Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If you will look at the first page at the top, it's addressed to all public security stations and it says: "We received a dispatch from the government of the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina and we hereby forward to you in full ..." If you look what's below it appears that they're forwarding that document that we just looked at, from Colonel Sajic which makes reference to the 01- -- the 1-92 decision of April 16th from the minister of defence. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes, can I see that. I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, I've ... However, I've not seen Stojan Zupljanin sign his name as the centre chief and then somebody called Dusko. I suppose that this was sent by the MUP communications system.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like you next to take a look at tab 7. This is 65 ter number 3362. And your first page in the B/C/S hard copy is simply a cover page which I think is translated into English as -- as "register," or "registry." Could you take a look at the second page in the B/C/S. Do you recognise the name of the person that signed on this document, which purports to be a registry for the Republika Srpska Presidency and National Assembly in Pale. Do you recognise the name?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes. That was a lady, Mrs. Rajka Stanisic. She worked in the office of the president of the Assembly, Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik, and the stamp also belonged to that office. But this is a copy from the log-book. To answer your question, I'd like to say that I did know Mrs. Rajka Stanisic personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I want to ask you, did you know a man named Dragan Kezunovic, who worked for communications in the RS MUP in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes, I did not see him that often. However, during the first few months, Mr. Kezunovic often visited our centre Colonel Kotlica, Milorad, was working with me, and he was the head of the cryptographic data protection, and he was an officer of the Ministry of Defence of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you about a man named Radovan Pejic who worked at the CSB Sarajevo for the RS MUP in 1992 in communications. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: I know Mr. Pejic from the Security Services Centre of Serbian Sarajevo. However, I only met him after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you for that --

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: I don't know if he worked there at the time or not. I didn't know him at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is would be a good time for me to break, if that's convenient for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, as I indicated earlier, we take breaks in the course of today, and now is the time for the first break. We will resume with your testimony when we return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before we continue with the witness, I just need to bring counsel up to date with where we are. I'll -- we'll let you know as we are told but as for tomorrow, for certain administrative reasons we couldn't adjust the scheduled afternoon sitting to the morning, so when we rise at 7.00 we would resume at 2.15 tomorrow afternoon. I will let you know what the position is, for the two following days, Wednesday and Thursday as soon as we are informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In connection with that, Your Honour, I should advise you that we have been informed that the next witness to follow this one won't be ready till Wednesday. He was called in anticipation of the estimated time for cross-examination of this witness that he wouldn't begin until that day, so I think he's only arriving tonight or tomorrow morning and won't be ready to begin before then. So we have as much time as we need tomorrow if we don't finish this witness today. And I alert you that in the event that there is something else that we may usefully spend or time on as a group or separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But he would be available by Wednesday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You may continue with your examination, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, next I would like you to take a look at the document that's in tab 4 of the binder. These are -- I will tell you. These are excerpts from a communications log-book which we have evidence that the -- the first -- the first 50 entries were for the RS MUP headquarters at Vrace in the beginning weeks of the war in April and May of 1992 and a later portion of the book was used by CSB Sarajevo. And so the first thing I want to ask you about is, I think it's page 4 in your hard copy. It's item number 18. Do you see there beside item 18 a reference that says: "MUP BiH." It's a report and it's sent to: Government, Serb republic?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, counsel. If could you please mention the number of the document for the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much and this is Exhibit P1428 in evidence. And the e-court page, I think is, 4 for both the English and bias.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Witness, for that interruption. Do you see the item I'm asking about?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Bear with me. 18? Report?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. To the government Serb republic and there's a phone number, 783460. Let me ask you; if a document were sent by CSB Sarajevo in late April of 1992, would it have gone to the MOD centre in Pale, if it was meant for the government of the Serb Republic; do you know?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: No. It should not have gone there. The stations all had their system of communications and they could send their dispatches directly to the government without those dispatches having to go through the MOD.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And to where would that document sent from MUP headquarters communications in Vrace have been sent to reach the government? To what person or what building?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: It would reach the secretary of the government. I can see a signature. I don't know who the signature belongs to. Whether it belongs to the courier or to the person who dispatched the dispatch. In any case, it would arrive at the desk of the secretary of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who would that be? What person; if you know.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: At the time, the secretary of the government was Mr. Nedeljko Vakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I know it's been a long time, but do you recognise that phone number, 783460?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: As for the number, 783460, we had a similar number to this one at our centre. I don't know whether that would be that number. I believe this is the fax number for the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where was that fax machine physically located in April and May of 1992; if you know? Was that in the MOD centre?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: We had our telefax at the centre and the government had its own fax machine on its premises. And so did all the police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know where the premises where the government and Presidency sat were in April and May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: The government and Presidency sat in Panorama Hotel, some of the staff. And the rest were at the Kikinda facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you look at the very next page at item 21 in that list of sent and received dispatches. You see it's sent by MUP Vrace, Sarajevo. It appears to be a summary, a security events report and it is sent to the president of the government at that same phone number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you've told us enough about that. Let me ask you to move on to -- I think you have to go on about five or six pages to find item number 81 and 82.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: These are --

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: These are dated the 18th of July, 1992. The first one is information on the work of MUP and military police. And the second is an order for establishment of mixed traffic check-points. There are to be sent to or given to SRBH staff. Can you tell me who that refers to in that context? That's the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but the staff of what? Is that the government? The Presidency? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what institution is meant by this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: I can see the word "staff."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My English translation translates farther as "Main Staff, security organ, Serbian army of the Serb BH." In July of 1992, the VRS was in existence. Can you tell us by what means and through which facilities a message from CSB Sarajevo would go to reach the Main Staff of the army? Would that go through MOD centre, or did the MUP have a direct connection from the CSB Sarajevo to the army?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: I am not familiar with the organisation of communications within the MUP. However, at that time, the MUP had a lot of problem with organising its system of communications. And I think that for a long time they didn't function properly and they could not protect information for a long time. And that's why our centre sometime provided services to them and held them with the transmission of certain documents to their end user. We used our communications system to do that. We had our own problems. Those were the first months of combat operations, and those communications systems would be down quite often. As I look at this document, I can't tell you anything else about it. This document doesn't emanate from my sector. Besides, I don't see in the document that the document was sent to our centre and then transmitted through our centre, the republic centre of communications, and cryptographic data protection. I really can't tell you how this was sent. This is a copy from a log-book. Somebody put a remark in order to confirm the receipt of the document and file it away. I don't know how they sent this document. This is a report or perhaps not. I don't even know that. I can't tell you because I don't see anything to indicate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you: Were you aware, did a CSB -- or particularly the CSB in Sarajevo have a direct communications link with the VRS in July of 1992, do you know? Or would they have go throughout MOD centre?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: In June, or July, rather, when if come to the MUP, I don't know whether the MUP had a direct communications link with the Main Staff or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I think it's three more pages to item number 1048. And, again, we're still looking at the communications log-book for CSB Sarajevo. And this is an item dated 7 November 1992. It's a solution to protect against fire and the issue of ownership of the Pale culture centre, sent to the Pale Municipal Assembly, the mayor, the president of the Executive Committee. Do you know if CSB Sarajevo for the MUP had a direct communications link to the political offices of the municipality in Pale or is that something that would go through your centre? I'm sorry, hold your answer for a minute while Mr. Zecevic raises a procedural matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I have -- I have a serious concern with the -- with the line of questions that my friend now is posing to this witness. One of the witnesses --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we ask the witness to take his headphones off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, could the witness please remove his headphones. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, one of the witnesses for the Office of the Prosecutor was a chief of the CSB Communication Department. Department of Communication of CSB Sarajevo. It was never put to him or -- or was he asked that, is there a connection between the CSB Sarajevo or General Staff or CSB Sarajevo and Pale? I simply do not understand the line of the -- of the questions that we are now asking the witness who doesn't obviously know anything about it, and when we had the first-hand knowledge from the witness who was here, none of these questions was asked of him. He was able to give us a -- a -- the best evidence about that. That is just my observation, Your Honours, and I don't really understand this -- where this line is taking us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Isn't the short answer to that, Mr. Zecevic, that if the witness is unable to answer the question that is being posed, he would say he doesn't know, and if the Prosecution has confused matters by the way they have led their evidence of the several witnesses then that is something that would -- I'm sure that Defence would not hesitate to remind the Chamber of when it comes to final submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The witness may replace his headphones, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I think my question was - I don't know if you recall - is, do you know whether or not CSB Sarajevo had a direct communications link to the political offices in Pale in November 1992 to the Pale Municipal Assembly or the mayor or the president of the Executive Committee. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: I cannot provide an answer to that question, because I don't know. But since they were at Pale, they could have used a courier to send some documents. It sounds logical. It is -- I don't know whether they had a direct communications link but they didn't need one, neither would the president of the municipality or the president of the Executive Committee. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. One more, or maybe two more. I think it's the next page, item number 1534 is -- the content is: Rejection of requests for vehicle. Referred to Ministry of Defence. Apparently sent to the RS Ministry of Defence. Was there a direct communications link between CSB Sarajevo and the Ministry of Defence, do you know? In December 1992?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: During that period, no. In December 1992 there were links between the communications centres, that is, the communications centre of the MUP and the com centre of the republic. But as the headquarters was at Pale, everything was carried by couriers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: I can see here that the request to be given a vehicle was denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. And then I think I have one more. I am afraid you have to go backwards. I want to find item number 292. And then we will be done with that tab. The sender is listed as the SR Presidency, it's a document numbered 01-518/92, dated 22 August 1992. The content: Accreditation of reports from the territory of SR. And the dispatch is given to apparently Mr. Borovcanin and Mr. Mitrovic and all the departments in the CSB Sarajevo, so this appears to be a document they received from the Presidency. Do you know how that document would have been transmitted from the Presidency in order to reach the CSB Sarajevo in August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic has a --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Witness, don't answer yet. We have a legal matter to discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's basically not legal. It's again an issue of interpretation. I believe the -- the original says --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Again, could we ask the witness to take his headphones off?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I? I believe the 292 document is accreditation of the reporters from the territory, not the reports. Accreditation of reporters on the territory of SR.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we have the witness put his headphones back on. I can ask him to help us with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, in terms of the -- the name of the document or the content of the document, could you read the B/C/S so we can get an interpretation? There's a question about what one of the words should say in English. Could you just read it out for us?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Serbian Republic, Presidency 01-518/92 of 22 August 1992. Accreditation of reporters from the territory of the Serbian republic. CSB Borovcanin, Mitrovic, all services.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And now could you answer my question: If this was sent from the Presidency to reach CS -- CSB Sarajevo, how would it go, if you know? Would that go through your centre or would it go from the Presidency directly to MUP headquarters or directly to the CSB, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: I cannot say, based on this register how exactly this document or letter was forwarded to the CSB; that is to Mr. Borovcanin and Mr. Mitrovic and all services, because this is a copy of a register that is unfamiliar to me, and I cannot know if any document with such a number was delivered to the centre at that time. From today's vantage point, I would be led to conclude that this document was not delivered this way from the Presidency to the CSB, but had to travel by another route. That is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And "by another route," what do you mean? Through whom or what?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Through a courier or through a regular exchange of mail. A courier could come from the Presidency and take the mail to the MUP. That would be the way. I cannot see from this that this document was dispatched in a different manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You cannot rule out that it was sent by electronic means or by radio or by fax from your centre to the MUP headquarters for furthering onto the CSB, can you?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: After so much time, I cannot be precise as to the way this document was handed over to the CSB because from the -- this registry and the sum review of incoming and outgoing mail, I cannot tell which route this took. Probably it was delivered by a courier, but that's an assumption of mine. Based on such registers as this, I cannot make accurate statements. I don't have the document in front of me, or anything else that has to do with accrediting reporters from the territory of the RS or the SR. If I had the document in front of me or the telegram, I may be able to say more. But as things stand, this is all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's see if can I help with one thing, one aspect. If we can look at tab 7; that's 65 ter 3362. This is the one that's described as the registry for the Presidency and the National Assembly that has a Ms. Rajka Stanisic's name on it. If you could turn to the page that has item number 01-518, the ERN is 0084-5621. I believe that's page 20 of the English in e-court and page 56 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: All right. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you see that item number is 01-51892 and it appears to be an accreditation of the -- my English says reports, but I think from the other it is probably "reporters" from the territory of RS dated 18th of August. This, indeed, appears to be that document that was referred to in the CSB Sarajevo log-book. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: It probably is. But I don't know the handwriting. And at the republican centre, no registers were kept -- no handwritten registers were kept. But, again, after so much time, I really cannot say anything about a document which was sent from the National Assembly and entered into their log-book. I'm not able to say anything about it because that document never reached me. I cannot say anything about its route either. If you wish to show me one of my log-books to show whether anybody sent it, then I may be able to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm again sorry. Maybe can you clarify with the witness, Mr. Hannis. 41, 7, I know that the witness didn't say that: "No handwritten registers were kept." He meant something completely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, it's been advised that your answer may have been misrecorded. At the beginning you said you didn't know the handwriting here in -- in this register for the Presidency and the National Assembly. And you said: "At the republican centre, no registers were kept, no handwritten registers were kept." Is that what you said, or did you say something else?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that no handwritten registers were kept but that I was unfamiliar with the handwriting in this register which is a register of the Assembly of the RS because they had their own registers and log-books; whereas at the centre, there were other log-books such as log-books of incoming telegrams or outgoing telegrams and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender 65 ter 3362.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: For what purpose exactly, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Because if I can just put my question: I'm not quite sure that I understand how this is relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, one of the contested issues that still remains in this case is the manner of communications within the Republika Srpska. This is a log-book kept regarding communications from the Presidency and from the National Assembly that were sent out throughout the Republika Srpska. I think you'll see there were over 2.000-some entries during the time period of the log-book. I've shown just one connection where a document that is in this log-book shows up in Exhibit P1428, the CSB Sarajevo log-book, demonstrating that it was dispersed down to the level of CSB. And that's just one example. But it's a contemporaneous log of those Presidency and National Assembly documents. You will see other links, and I don't think there's any question about the authenticity of this document. This was seized by Mr. Pat Treanor and two investigators from the OTP in December 1997 from a Mr. Milos Vukasinovic, who -- an official of the RS Ministry of Justice. So I think we've shown authenticity, and I think from my comments, there is relevance and probative value particularly on the issue of communications and communications between alleged members and participants of the joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do object. First of all, the witness -- this witness has nothing to do with this log-books [sic], never saw them, it was not within his purview, never had these documents before, so he cannot give us any kind of indication to the authenticity of these documents or provenance or whatever. Now, the second thing, if my learned friend suggests that this -- this particular document or dispatch, the accreditation of the reporters was sent to MUP, I would like to know where did he found that reference, from this log-book. Because this log-book does not contain the -- the -- the intended recipient of the -- of any of the documents. We don't know even -- even if that's -- even if that's a log-book of all the documents that were prepared. Maybe some were sent, maybe some were not. Really, on the basis of such a scarce information that we have from the contents of this document as it appears right now, I don't think we can -- that it reaches the threshold to be admitted. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I reply? Your Honours, this witness has identified Ms. Rajka Stanisic as the employee who worked for the -- as a secretariat for the National Assembly. She is the person identified on the cover of the register. It is logical that she would be a person to keep this book. I didn't really hear a response to what I said about where this document was seized and who it was seized from. I guess I'm asking if my learned friend has a serious objection about whether this document is authentic. We -- we haven't listed Ms. Stanisic as a witness because we have a limited number of witnesses to call. And if he wants a document that goes to MUP, there is one at item number 180, which is from President Karadzic ordering that two platoons of special police forces report to Tomo Kovac, so there are documents like that referred to within this registry. That document would be 65 ter 1581, not on my list to be used with this witness but a document contained within the register log; that's 65 ter 3362.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: As I understand it, Mr. Hannis, I don't think that there is any challenge to the provenance or authenticity. I shouldn't say provenance, authenticity of the proposed exhibit. The reservation that I have is that we're dealing with a document which, arguably, is illustrative or an example of these communications going back and forth. But the -- its admission as an exhibit would form the basis for submissions and argument down the road, and my question is: How does this add to -- how does this assist the Chamber beyond similar documents which we already have no shortage of? That's -- that's my difficulty, Mr. Hannis. It appears to be somewhat vague and insubstantial by itself and it doesn't assist to add it at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I feel that I am letting you down because I haven't been able to persuade you. I would think that in a document-heavy case like this, you would relish the opportunity to have a document like this, which has 2100 documents from the Presidency and the Assembly all in one place, listed by numbers, which will help you cross refreshes them when you find them appearing in other places. It has some descriptions of persons that you have heard testify here which will corroborated some of their evidence about when they went on a trip somewhere because there will be a travel order for that witness on or about that date when he says that he was at a meeting in Zvornik, for example. I -- and it's all conveniently located in one document. If I can't persuade you now, I'll try to do it through a written submission in the bar table motion. But I would think this is something that you would like to have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just one clarification. I'm not -- it was my understanding that Mr. Hannis is offering this document, and I believe Your Honours commented accordingly, as -- as a log-book of communications. I would like that clarification from Mr. Hannis. Is Mr. Hannis saying this document is the log-book of communications coming from the Presidency and the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm saying it's a registry of documents from the Presidency and the Assembly, and I'm saying other evidence will show that these documents moved through means of communication to other participants of the alleged joint criminal enterprise. And some of the communication's contents itself related to actions that we say were part of the joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you heard our objection anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that the document may be received as an exhibit and therefore admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01723, Your Honours. Your Honours, the 65 ter number is 03362. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I would now, Witness, like you to take a look at the document that's at tab 8 of the binder you have there. You mentioned you would like us to try and talk about some log-books from the republican centre. This is 65 ter 1303. Do you recognise that cover page? It's telegrams -- log for telegrams to be transmitted over the radio between April and November 1992.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we can go into private session for one or two questions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in private session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sir, is -- are these pages that were copied out of that republic centre log-book and given by you to investigators from the OTP back in 1998, I believe?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that it was that way, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And after that meeting - I think it was in February 1998 where you gave these few pages to the OTP investigators - do you know what happened to the original log-book from which these pages come?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: In 1998, when the authorities moved from Pale to Banja Luka, the Ministry of Defence also was moved to Banja Luka. Part of the documents were taken to Banja Luka and others remained in use at the centre at Pale until around 2004, when the centre was searched and some documents pertaining to the war period from 1992 through 1996 were seized and taken probably to the office of the ICTY in Sarajevo or Nedzarici to be precise. Assistance was provided by the staff the CSB Sarajevo with -- the headquarters of which was at Pale. The team leader was there too. I don't need to mention his name. We -- I can tell that by looking at the signature on the document. And some of the documents were taken away during that period; whereas, the other portion of the document was handed over to the municipalities when the Ministry of Defence of the RS and the Ministry of Defence of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina became -- were merged to become a single Ministry of Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Those documents were then given to Banja Luka and the municipalities. Where those documents are, since it happened five or six years ago, well, they may be in some office probably, at least I can draw that conclusion from the information I have at the office of the old headquarters, or they were also moved to Banja Luka. I don't know exactly what happened to the documents, but some documents probably still remain at the old site of the fire-fighting building, which was the seat of the monitoring and information centre at Pale. This is an excerpt from the log-book of radio communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you have not seen -- you have not seen the original from which these excerpts came since 19 -- well, since they went to Banja Luka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: This log-book of telegrams was kept at the republican centre in Pale. I recognised the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. But my question was: You have not seen the original since it went to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: The republican centre in Pale has not been in function since 1998. And the centre stopped working in 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: And it --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. My question is: You have not seen the original telegram log-book from which these excerpts came since they -- since the original went to Banja Luka; correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: I have not seen them since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me --
