utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Since the documents were handed over, I have not seen them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Look at the excerpt, page -- number 190, item 190, dated 13 July 1992. The sender is Bijeljina and the addressee is Banja Luka. Did this telegram go through your centre from Bijeljina to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how about item number 192. 14 July, regarding surrender of weapons. The sender is the Presidency, and it's to all municipalities around Gorazde. It says: "Delivered to the municipalities." I take it this was a telegram that was sent out throughout MOD centre in Pale?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes. This document was sent through the republican communications and cryptographic protection centre, the centre where I was the chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, maybe we should have a redaction for that last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if I could tender --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for the record, there will be no need for redaction since we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't realise we were still in private session. That's good. I would like to tender 65 ter 1303.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01724, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stay in private session then for the next question. If you could look at the next tab, number 10 -- I'm sorry, number 9; this is 65 ter 2914. Witness, have you seen this document before? It's dated the 18th of June 1992 from the Minister of Defence, Bogdan Subotic?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: The minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And in it he says the communications centre at Pale can send telegrams to the Serbian Autonomous Region of Krajina and to other Serbian autonomous regions. And his message is directed to the ministries of the government. Is that communications centre that is he referring to the one of which you were the chief in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: The English version -- oh I see, on the other side. I'm -- I don't speak English. This is not the minister of the interior; it's the minister of defence who signed, Colonel Bogdan Subotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There must've been a miscommunication. But, yes. Colonel Subotic. And the communications centre in Pale that he refers to in this document, that's the centre where you were the chief in 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to tendered 65 ter 2914.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01725, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Indeed, your centre could, and did, send telegrams for other ministries besides the Ministry of Defence in 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next I want to ask you know a man named Nebojsa Savic, who used to work for the SUP in Sarajevo, in Sarajevo CSB before the war. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: I didn't know him before the war, but Nebojsa Savic showed up in Pale during the war, so I had the opportunity of meeting him. I didn't see him very often. I might have seen him on a couple of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are we in open session now, Your Honours? I have lost track.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We're in private.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Could we go into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us where the republic communications centre for the Republika Srpska was physically located in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: The republic communications centre of Republika Srpska was at the fire station in Koran.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is --

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: In Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I would like you to take a look at the document that's at tab 12 in your binder. It's 65 ter 1938.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I realise I'm getting near the end of my allotted time, if I haven't reached it, but given that the original one and a half hours that the Court allowed for direct examination was at a time when we thought the witness was going to be here live and now he is on videolink, there is some inherent extra time built into doing a videolink examination. I'd like to ask if I can have another 20 minutes or so to finish with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You will see this document appears to be a statement of Nebojsa Savic given to representatives of the State Security Service on or about the 9th of September, 1992. I will note for Your Honours that in the English translation the date of 9/9/1992 is missing from the first paragraph. It is in the original of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I -- I -- I suspect that Mr. -- Mr. Hannis is going to offer the statement as an exhibit, if I correctly understand. But, in any case, this is the statement of another person. I don't see how can we admit it through this -- through this witness, despite the fact that he knows this person by name. I don't -- I don't really see the connection, the nexus between these two. And if I correctly remember, we had a long conversation about this when the Office of the Prosecutor was actually opposing our -- our line of questions where we wanted to -- to -- to -- to talk to the witness about the -- the contents of the statements which he, himself, took, and then the Office of the Prosecutor was -- was opposing that, as not being a proper line. Therefore, if -- if Mr. Hannis is going to introduce this as -- as -- or try to introduce this as an exhibit, I believe I gave my reasons for the objection. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I may, could I ask the witness to take his headphones off. I need to be precise about some things. Yes, as I recall, I personally raise as fuss when the Defence was trying to introduce certain Official Notes that were taken at Omarska. And I don't think that any of them that they were trying to introduce were taken by the witness who was actually testifying. They were not signed by the persons who gave the statements. And they weren't statements. They were Official Notes which was part of the way, I guess, the Trial Chamber decided that you would be able to admit those in the face of my argument that they shouldn't come in, because, in effect, they were statements of absent witnesses. So I would be pretty red in the face if I got up now and tried to say, You, we should admit this statement of a witness. But there are two essential differences between this statement of a witness and those Official Notes of detainees at Omarska. There's no indication or suggestion or reason to believe that this witness, a Serb who is being debriefed after his release from captivity by Muslims, was beaten by any MUP members of Serb ethnicity; and, in addition, this witness signed the statement. However, I'm not intending to introduce a statement, but I'm planning to read certain portions of what this witness said to ask if this witness can confirm some or part of what he says about what happened at the communications centre in Pale and setting up a communications network in the RS in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, not to mention that I have a great problem when we are talking about -- what -- what I -- what I see as a problem is that the Office of the Prosecutor keeps -- keeps dividing the -- the victims from -- from -- from the different sides by their ethnicity. I just don't see why -- why is that relevant at all if the victim is whoever, whichever ethnicity it belongings to, but apart from that, I don't think that Mr. Hannis can use this statement to ask the witness. He can openly ask the witness about the certain event if he wants to find out whether the witnesses knows about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Which is precisely the question I was just about to ask Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, aren't you unnecessarily complicating the matter by using the statement which you said you aren't going seek to exhibit? Just ask the witness -- wouldn't it be simpler to just ask the witness the relevant question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I would like to show that I have a good-faith basis for my questions, that there is a source document for where I'm coming up with questions. But you are right, I will just ask some questions. If we can have the witness put his headphones back on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, were you aware that Mr. Nebojsa Savic moved a certain short-wave radio station to -- from the Panorama Hotel to the fire brigade where the republican communications centre was located in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware that Mr. Savic met with --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry. I believe the witness is looking at the document, so the document should be taken away from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He said he didn't know. But that's fine. He can set the document aside.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, were you aware that Mr. Nebojsa Savic met with Colonel Kotlica in the communications centre in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: I was aware of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you know that the two of them were working on communications plans for connecting the Crisis Staff of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina with the autonomous regions?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is leading questions [sic], Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Calls for a yes-or-no answer. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Let's get on with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know, sir?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: I didn't know about that. I wasn't a member of any party. I was an officer in the Territorial Defence and in the monitoring an information centre. I wasn't a member of any party, so whether there were contacts between the late Colonel Milorad Kotlica and Mr. Nebojsa -- what was his last name? I don't know. I know there were some contacts but to what effect, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let me show you one more document. This is at tab 14. It's 65 ter 1305. This is a document dated April 1993. It's from the VRS. It's an analysis of the combat readiness and activities of the Army of the Republika Srpska in 1992. And I think I will skip to the second page that you have, which should have a chart at the top of the page. It's Figure 4. Okay? Did you find that? The chart is entitled: "The use of the PTT and military automatic telephone exchanges outside the Army of Republika Srpska." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we be given the indication which page I was supposed we supposed to [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... page 36 of the English in e-court and it's page 33 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a couple of questions about some of the entities listed in the chart. Can you tell us about the Sokolac Warning and Reporting Centre? Was that a subordinate to the republic centre in Pale?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in the paragraph immediately under the chart I want to read and ask you a question. It says: "In addition to PTT links of great importance within the system of communications of the army were the communications of the very developed warning and reporting centres in the territory of RS. Most of the 67 of such centres are linked with the military communications system, and they have played a major role, to date, in warning and reporting communications, in particular the Pale Warning and Reporting Centre." That is the communications centre in Pale that we have been talking about this afternoon; correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last thing, sir, I'd like to show you tab 15. It's Exhibit P1319. I wonder, if you have a pen that you could use for marking. I'd like, if you could, just on that map of the Pale area mark four locations for me. First of all, with the number 1 and a circle around it, the approximate location of the Pale Republican Communications Centre in 1992 in the fire station. I know it's not the biggest map in the world, but if could you give us an approximate location.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: This map is not very accurate, but the republic centre could be under the number 1. Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Number 2, are you able to locate on there the approximate location of Kalovita Brda?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Kalovita Brda? I can, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. That's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May that be given an exhibit number and admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, the marked version of P1319 shall be given Exhibit P01726, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my colleague, Mr. Cvijetic, is suggesting that maybe this would be an appropriate moment to take the break and then we can start after the break immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, although it is nine minutes early, I think it would probably be more efficient to shift the time that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: I didn't hear you. I apologise. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, you were affiliated with the Secretariat of National Defence at Pale up to April 1992, right?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes. I worked at the Territorial Defence and then I joined the secretariat, and I worked there at Pale until 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You said that at the moment when the regional centre was established in the fire brigade hall at Pale, that, for a while, you also had communications with the centre in Sarajevo, right?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: I said that when the republican centre had been established, not the regional centre at Pale. The rest of us were part of the organisational scheme and we were part of the organisation, together with the city centre in Sarajevo. I believe that that was the Federation centre, or the centre affiliated with the Federation, while Sarajevo was still one city; when it was not divided.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let's just clarify one thing. That communications centre, that belonged to the city of Sarajevo with which you were linked, as you say, that was under the control of the Muslim forces, right?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: When we were part of the line of command of the city centre, that was before the conflict started. In 1992, in the month of April, we remained linked with the same city centre and we could still communicate with them freely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The city centre with which you communicated in April 1992, that centre was under the control of the Muslim forces, right?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown a document, 1D04-3886. Tab number 10 in our binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is an order which was signed by the commander of the Territorial Defence, or, rather, the staff of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Colonel Hasanefendic. Do you see the document?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is that a document that, in April 1992, you received at your republican centre at Pale?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes, that's the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, I assume that you received that document pursuant to the existence of your links and communications with the centre in Sarajevo, right?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I remember correctly, in the statements that you provided to the OTP, your comment was that when you had seen this order issued by Colonel Hasanefendic on the 29th of April, 1992, that you lost all hope that the conflict would be restricted and that it would come to a peaceful resolution.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes. I received that document at the centre by means of a teleprinter communication from the city staff or rather, from the republican centre which was on the Federation side. They believed that they could send this type of documents and orders in order to put pressure on us who were part of their organisation until the beginning of combat activities. I received a second document as well, however, that second document arrived from Banja Luka. In other words, there were two identical documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that the contents of both documents were identical? But we are still talking about one and the same document that was signed by the commander of the Territorial Defence, Colonel Hasan Efendic. However, you received it from two different sources. One came from Banja Luka; and the other came from Sarajevo, right?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you received this document, or, rather, this order, and you understood that to be the beginning of very serious armed conflicts in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes. When we received this document, I personally handed that document to the president of the republic. And the second copy went to the then-commander, General Kukanjac. Again, I delivered it personally to him. When I spoke to the gentlemen from the OTP, I asked them to show me this document which was first went missing but then it was discovered and I asked them to explain item number 4 to me, because there is a reference to combat activities in there. And that's when I lost all hope that there would be a peaceful solution to the conflict that had just started. Because their number one man, the commander of the BiH army, ordered foot soldiers to launch attacks across the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to remove the civilian population which means that this was, de facto, a declaration of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: However, this document is something that you received and you took it to President Karadzic first and General Kukanjac, the commander of the 5th Military District of the JNA; did I understand you properly?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D00397, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, my learned friend Mr. Hannis asked you about the communications systems. That was earlier today. Do you remember that? He asked you about the existence of different communications systems.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You listed three different systems: One belonged to the MUP and it was the MUP communication system; the second one was the communications system which you worked within, that was the Territorial Defence or rather the Ministry of Defence communications system; and the third system was the military communications system. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: There was an independent system which belonged to the Ministry of the Interior. The second system was the system of the armed forces and the third system was the communications systems which belonged to the civilian authorities -- or, rather, it belonged to the Ministry of Defence but was used by the civilian authorities. And the third system carried out tasks given to it by the civilian authorities under civilian power and that was the republican communications centre with all of its subordinated centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, the fact is that all those three communications systems were independent of each other. They worked independently, right?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, when you, within your system, which was the system of the Ministry of Defence, when you wanted to establish any kind of communication to send confidential telegrams, you were first supposed to contact the opposing side, the receiving side, and provide them with code -- the so-called code keys; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a document. It is 1D04-3893. Tab 14 in your binder. This document was signed by the minister of defence, Colonel Bogdan Subotic. You can see it, can't you?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we do not have a date on the document. However, if I remember it correctly, in one of your statements provided to the OTP or somewhere else, you confirmed that the first telegrams that you could send from the centre at Pale to your regional centres under seal, as it were, that it was only towards the end of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes, thereabouts. Sometime around the 20th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This document reflects what we have just said. Before you started using a communication with sealed telegrams, you were supposed to establish prior communication with all the centres listed here. You had to physically get in touch in them and convey the key codes to them.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And this order reflects that and goes along the same lines, right?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And it says here that the document should be sent to the six listed regions in the Territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as it was called at the time?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this document at all, sir?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes. I remember the document and I remember the code-name Vatra or fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I'd like to tender the document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection, although we don't have a date, as he indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D00398, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I suppose that this document was drafted sometime in the month of June 1992, because, if, in late June 1992, you managed to start sending telegrams to at least some of the regional centres, that would mean that prior to that, those codes had been submitted to them in keeping with the document that is before you, right?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, the code keys that you delivered to the regional centres in the territory, you delivered those key -- code keys only to them and not anybody else.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes. That went along the line of command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your code keys were specific for your communications system and they made sense and they could be used only in your communication system, right?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Likewise, the military communication system also had its own code keys that they delivered to their regional units or communications centre in order to be able to communicate?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes, the military had its own system of communications and they used those communication systems to communicate. However, we knew that we could also exchange our code books. I don't know whether this was done pursuant to this document or not. Sometime at a later period, we made use of that. They didn't. They never did. But we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The fact is that every communication system had its own code keys which differed from one system to the next. And on the basis of their own code key, they established communication with the regional parts of that communication system, right?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And, in that sense, if you didn't know, if you were not familiar with code keys, you would not be able to read the contents of a message, and that's how you made sure that the message did not fall into unwanted hands. That was the whole purpose of the code keys, right?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, this gentleman, Kotlica, before the war, and before the hostilities started sometime in April 1992, he was an assistant commander of the Territorial Defence of the Socialist Federative Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and he was in charge of the communications system there?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Colonel Kotlica was the head of communications in the former Secretariat of National Defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which means that he was at the -- at a level of an assistant minister. He was a military official within the administration for communications and cryptographic protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: He was a member of the Secretariat, or rather he was affiliated with the republican Secretariat for National Defence. Today, that would be the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And due to very well known circumstances, he was transferred to Pale but he remained working at the Ministry of Defence of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes, he was affiliated with the same centre where I was and he was the head of communications and cryptographic protection of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The fact is, sir, is it not that that some of the documents that you dispatched due to the situations which you explained for us which was very difficult when it comes to communications and maintaining the system of communications, you used -- used different ways and means to communicate with municipalities and regional centres and that depended on what was available to you at the time and how you could communicate with those centres at the time.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will show you another document for illustration. 1D04-3910. That's tab 12. This document is dated 14 July 1992 and in the signature block we see the name of the late Colonel Milorad Kotlica. Basically, this is forwarding a message of the president of the Presidency, Radovan Karadzic. Do you remember this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In this document, the president of the Presidency, Dr. Karadzic, in mid-July 1992: "Orders the presidents of the municipalities that in all villages in which the Croatian Bosnian population surrender their weapons and show no intention of fighting us, must enjoy the full protection of Serbian state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The municipality presidents must be held accountable for that." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And after that, the telegram was dispatched to the municipalities in various ways. Over the phone, by teleprinter, by radio communication or radio relay communications. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This illustrates the problem, that you did not -- or you could not communicate with every municipality in the same manner. Depending on the time.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. The system of communications was disrupted and it was very difficult to dispatch any telegram, especially during that period that encompassed the first few months after the beginning of the hostilities and then we tried to manage whichever we way could. We used teleprinters, radio communications and other times of communication. But, we did use code tables and with great efforts, we were able to do the work but some telegrams never made it to their intended recipients.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken you said you remember the document and you also remember the signature of the late Milorad Kotlica, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes, this is his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there is no opposition I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I do have an objection. This document has something on the top called "The Hague against Justice Revisited, document number 7" I think this is from some -- publication of a group that was preparing a Defence for Radovan Karadzic. There's no stamp on the document, so I don't know where The Hague against Justice Revisited got this document. That's the essence of my complaint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That apart, Mr. Hannis, hasn't the witness confirmed that he remembers?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He says he remembers it is but I don't know from when or where he remembers it. Does he remember it from seeing it in this book or does he remember it from seeing it in Pale in 1992? We need some further elaboration on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you the following: The document which we're discussing now, dated 14 July 1992, do you remember seeing this document in 1992; and, if so, where?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: The document dated 14 July 1992 was brought to the republican centre of communications and cryptographic protection where I worked by a courier. And in 1997 or 1998, when I met the investigators of the ICTY, when I and General Bogdan Subotic gave our first statements in the investigative procedure to the investigators of the ICTY, I gave this document to Mr. John Ralston, who then was an investigator, because they demanded these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that at the time you gave them a copy of this document -- just a minute, let me finish. Which did not have these indications as -- that we see here, document number 7, and the association, The Hague Against Justice Revisited and so on.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: It was just this same telegram, but without this title document number 7. I showed them the original document and they copied it and took it to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I hope that satisfies the requirement by Mr. Hannis. If I can have the 1Dnumber, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As exhibit 1D00399, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you know that Mr. Kezunovic who was assistant minister of the interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was a friend and acquaintance of the late Colonel Kotlica, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes, I know that he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that you stated today that Mr. Kezunovic on several occasions came to your centre to consult and discuss the problems they, just as you, faced with the functioning of the communications system, right?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes. Especially with regard to the disrupted state of that system.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the communications system of the MUP - and I mean the MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina - initially was established at Vrace. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes. They had some of their communications system there in the former school building. I mean the MUP school at Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And after that, the communications centre of the CSB of Sarajevo was partly moved to Lukavica. Do you know that? Or another building anyway at Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes, something like that. But I don't exactly remember where they went.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You know that Mr. Kezunovic worked on the establishment of the centre at Pale and that at some time in the summer of 1992, they moved the communications centre again but this time to Bijeljina, right?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: As far as Mr. Kezunovic is concerned, I didn't speak to him about the establishment of any centres. But the then-chief of that communication centre at Pale was my friend, the late Milenko Paunovic. And for that reason, we had good communication and we assisted each other in some segments where he was unable to do something, we helped him do so. But not in all situations. We had a disrupted communications system but he also complained about serious problems that they had in communication. And when they came to Pale, they had problems with the facility at Kikinda and the facility at Kalovita Brda where part of the communication system was, because the infrastructure was limited and they could not establish sufficient communications to cater for a stationary communication centre. They had huge problems. Only very late did they start to function under more or less normal conditions because it was extremely difficult, especially in their segment of the communications system.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, let us go through some documents shown to you by Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown document number 5 -- or, rather, under tabs 5 and 6. And I mean P467 and P555.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember that a short while ago you spoke with Mr. Hannis about this document? It's a document of the regional Secretariat of National Defence, dated 4 May 1992. And it was signed by Lieutenant-Colonel Milorad Sajic pursuant to the decision of the ministry that you saw earlier, the Ministry of National Defence, I mean. He ordered general mobilisation. Do you remember the document? You saw it some two hours ago.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes, I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then Mr. Hannis showed you another document, tab 6 in his binder and that's document P555, bearing the same date, and it's a MUP document. Remember that too?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was put to you then that these are two identical documents with regard to their contents. The MUP was dispatching it to their regional stations using their communication system that. That's what was put to you, right?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at the second page of this document, sir. On page 1, we saw the decision with its five items. And here, there's a reasoning which also includes five items. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the last item, item 5 says that this decision takes effect forthwith. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And it's signed: Regional Secretariat for National Defence, Lieutenant-Colonel Milorad Sajic. Now, please take another look at document P476 [as interpreted], which is tab 5, and please focus on page 2 on the reasoning. I'm referring to tab 5 in the Prosecution binder and the document number is P467. We saw it a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's turn to page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you see, sir, that, here, the reasoning of this decision has only four items. The fifth one is missing.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So, the documents are not identical after all, are they?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, I'll show you another document. P1723. It's tab 7 in the Prosecution binder. It's that log-book allegedly kept by one Rajka Stanisic. It's the log-book of the Republika Srpska Presidency and National Assembly. Let us go to page 00845673. Please ask the usher to turn to that page.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Found.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I remember you said that you hadn't seen this log-book before but you commented on it with Mr. Hannis, so I would like to comment on it too. 021098 is the item number. And it's the first entry on this page, right?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And it says, under narrative: "Travel order for Radovan Colovic," I believe?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Then the fourth item from the top 01-1101, can you see that entry?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It says: "Approval for fuel."

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And underneath, 1101 again, it says: "Fuel for the villa of the" -- either Presidency or president. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this document has nothing to do with the communications log-book. This is a register of the documents of the Presidency and the National Assembly, right?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, thank you very much. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We don't have question for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If we could look first at ... what's now been marked -- mm-hm. Sorry, Your Honours, I'm having trouble finding the reference. It's the document from Colonel Efendic, which is dated the 29th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned receiving this document, actually, two versions of this document; one from Sarajevo and one from Banja Luka. From whom, or from what entity in Banja Luka, did you receive a copy of Efendic's order? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: I received this document from Sarajevo, from the former republic communications centre located in the building of the former Executive Committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that --

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Which now houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I understand that, but I thought you went on to say that you also received a second copy from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: We received the second one, yes. We received the second one from Banja Luka. The second one which was identical to this one, we received from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question is from whom or what in Banja Luka? From the MUP? From your regional centre? From the army? From whom?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: From the centre it says here "Banja Luka SUP." It bears their number, and they sent it to us because they had received this document -- the first to receive it was the municipal centre which received it from the BH government, the former republic centre in Sarajevo. And it was sent to Sanski Most, to 45484. And then this same telegram was sent from the teleprinter of the Banja Luka SUP, 45254 is the number, and was sent to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So you had --

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: As you can see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You had telegraphic connections with Banja Luka on the 29th of April; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: It was a teletyping communication. It was open text. If you will allow me, I have a book here written by Colonel Hasanefendic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: And it's called --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not interested in a book by Colonel Efendic. If that's something that the Defence wanted to ask you about, they could. I just need to address a couple of particular things that they asked you about. At page 60, line 22 today, you were asked about -- I'm sorry. Page 62, line 5, you were asked about the three communications systems of -- for the Ministry of Defence, the Ministry of the Interior, and the army or the VRS system. You said that they all worked independently. Did your centre in the MOD have a direct communication link with either the MUP communications centre or the VRS communications centre in 1992? Did you have direct communication links with either of them?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Later communication was established between the two centres, direct communication, manual communication, after certain technical conditions were put in place for such communications to be established. But not in the first few months. There was a courier service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And did you not have telephone communication with either of those systems in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: We did have telephone communications, regular PTT lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you had fax communication as well, right?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes, we did have all PTT communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At what point in time in 1992 did you begin to share cryptographic documents with either the army or the MUP; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: I already said that: Around the 20th of June, 1992. I can't tell you the exact date but it was around the 20th of June. June, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, I wanted to ask you a question about that. That was tab 14 of the Defence binder. Did that get an exhibit number? Yes, it's 1D398. Could we have a look at that for a second? You see the -- the top of the page. And it has a registry number, 21-33.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know what that number refers to? What's -- what's the 21 refer to? Is that Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: No, it's not. This is a log-book which was in the republic centre --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: -- and an operative wrote that number in hand. It's a number from the log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So does 21 refer to that communications centre? And 33 is the 33rd document sent in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we don't know the date because it doesn't appear to be here on the original. Could we look at Exhibit P1725. This is the one you saw earlier from Minister Subotic advising the ministries about the capability of sending telegrams to the autonomous regions, et cetera. And you see the number on that one? That is 21-72, and it's dated the 18th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry -- I'm sorry, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we have the witness take off his headphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I wanted to suggest that. I'm sorry. I'm not aware if the witness have taken the headphones off. Okay. Your Honours, I believe there is a difference between the numbers. The first one, this is -- this is -- the first one -- the first document was strictly confidential document number 33. 21/33. This is obviously not a strictly confidential document so there might be --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's not in evidence. That has not been established yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. But what I'm say something that you are -- I anticipate your question would be 72 and 33 and those are probably the two different log-books. That is what I'm just suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's for a submission. That's not an objection to my question. Could we -- I don't know what Your Honours ruling is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have the witness put his headphones back on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have P1725 in front of you? That 18 June document from Minister Subotic?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you see that was numbered 21-72. Does that not suggest to you that 21-33 must have been sent sometime far in advance of the 18th of June?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Isn't that a submission rather than asking the witness to -- you're asking the witness for a conclusion, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, he seems to be a person in position to perhaps be able to give us one. If he doesn't know, he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I don't know why I'm instinctively troubled by the form of that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. May I should just ask an open-ended question and say: Do you have any idea of how you might correlate a date for item number 21-33 if the document sent on 20 June is 21-72?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Perhaps if would be more helpful because the issue is the reconciliation of these two apparently conflicting documents so to the extent that the witness can assist the Chamber in this regard, I suppose the way the question is now phrased may be more helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you understand the question I'm asking you now or I do need to rephrase it, ask it again?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: For your question, I can give you my opinion, an answer which might not correspond with reality. According to the rules of office work, this number, 21, might have been assigned to the Ministry of Defence, and General Bogdan Subotic at the time was minister of defence so it could that be this was the classification number of the Ministry of Defence. I don't know exactly. But that would have been the logic of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that. But my understanding about the way that documents are then numbered within the ministry are they're sequential, so the first document sent in 1992 would be number 1, and so on, up through 100 or 1.000. 72 would be sent at some date after 33. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes. Only I don't have the log-book here in which this document was recorded. This is probably a log-book that was kept at the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand ...

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: And that's the -- that's the number of the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I -- I share your pain in missing the log-book, sir. Let me ask you about the code systems. You talked a little bit about the code keys. And at page 64, line 13 in your answer you said: "Yes, the military had its own system of communications. And they used those communications systems to communicate. However, we knew that we could also exchange our code books. Sometime at a later period we made use of that." Do you mean you exchanged code books with the military in 1992? 1992; and, if so, can you tell us when that was?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: In 1992, we had certain documents which we used to work with the army. We shared the same documents. We had documents we used to send certain orders and other documents to the army, and they had the same document to decode what we sent and then decide what was being sent to which end user.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recall when that was, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: The republic centre in Pale started sending information using cryptographic data protection sometime around the 20th of June, and it was one of the centres that played a great role in the communications system of the VRS, because it communicated between the army and the civilian authorities in the government and other structures as necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever exchange code books with the Ministry of Interior in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: We didn't have a developed code system with the Ministry of Interior, but based on certain documents, if necessary, we were able to carry out exchanges. But that was in the later period, that we were able to communicate using the same documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you say "the later period," when do you mean, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: After they had managed to establish their centres and when they were able to use -- to work with full capacity and to service their communications, which, as I said, was limited, because of technical difficulties. They didn't have the capacity to communicate with everybody. It was later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But having exchanged code documents with both the army and the MUP, did your centre then have the capability to send coded communications for either the army or the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were able to do that. However, since the MUP was close to our centres, it was not necessary for us to encode anything because it consumed too much time. We sent the documents via couriers because we had a courier system. However, for example, between the army and the MUP and not only the MUP but the government of the RS and others, we were able to receive certain regular reports and then send them to the addresses marked on them, including the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Or the ministry of finance are or anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Next, I wanted to ask you about tab 12. This is the document dated 14th of July signed by Colonel Kotlica, and I don't know what exhibit number it got. I think it's 1D399, yes. This apparently is one particular document that you show -- that you chose to show the OTP investigators when you and Mr. Subotic spoke with them, when, back in 1997 or 1998? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes. There was a meeting in the -- December of 1997 and the second one was on the 10th of January, I believe, of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall why you chose this particular document to show to the OTP investigators?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: I don't remember that now. They asked to copy some documents, so these documents were provided to them. I wasn't personally present when they made the copies. They had their own people. They came to the former building of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you have the document in front of you right now?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It -- it seems to be in an unusual format. It -- it doesn't have any -- any number on it, so do you have any explanation for that? There's no registry number either from the Presidency's registry or from the com centre. Is that unusual?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: I remember this document, and I remember that there was some problems regarding certain groups which came into conflict with the then-Muslim and now-Bosniak population in certain areas and for that reason, as communication was very difficult at the time, a telegram arrived to be sent to all these municipalities to protect all the population who have expressed their loyalty and surrendered their weapons. It related to people who had no intention to oppose the Army of the VRS and these people were to be protected. They were to enjoy the full protection in the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I remember that. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: This telegram, because communications were difficult, this telegram was sent by telephones, teletype -- via teletyping in any way that was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: It was very difficult for us to carry out this task, but in the end, we managed to send it to all the addressees.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But in your documents that you gave the OTP, which is now Exhibit P1724. Item number 192 is dated the 14th of July. It's about the surrender of weapons from the Presidency to all municipalities around Gorazde. So that sounds like that's the same document that you have in front of you right now. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: I apologise. What was the number again?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, if you want to see where it is it in your log-book, that's Exhibit P1724, which was tab 8 today. And it's item number 192.

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: I can see it now, yes. 192, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: That's the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... from the log-book of telegrams to be transmitted over the radio. Would you agree that this log entry appears to be referring to this document dated the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes. Here, under 192. This log-book, since the original log-books were missing, this log-book comprises quite a few pages of A4 papers and all the entries were made by hand. A log-book of that kind existed at the centre, and it is true that that particular thing was recorded under this number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question is: Do you have any idea why there is no document number on this, either number 192 from your communications log-book, or a number from the RS Presidency and Assembly registry of documents? Is that normal?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: I can't give you any comment as to why there's no number, whether it was omitted or what, I'm sure that this telegram was dispatched to all the addressees and I'm sure that you will be able to find this telegram in the files of some of the municipalities, in their archives. I'm sure that it was sent. We did not have any archives. We were just the department that received telegrams and dispatched telegrams to the end users.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm almost done with this document. Can you explain for us who this document is intended to be for? The original message is from President Karadzic to the municipalities about surrendering weapons. But on the bottom of it it appears that Colonel Kotlica has added the information about delivering documents. Where is this document supposed to be registered in your communications centre or at the Presidency or somewhere else? It seems an odd combination that Colonel Kotlica has put this information on and typed his name, but there's no indication that he is mailing it back to the president to let him know or sending it to the file. Can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Under 192, the handwritten entry, this is not the handwriting of the late Milorad Kotlica. This is the handwriting of one of the operatives who was employed at the radio department. The -- those telegrams, according to the logic of the matter, should have been registered with the presidents of the municipalities. Because the presidents of the municipalities were instructed to protect the Croatian and Muslim populations which had been involved in the activities described in the dispatch. Those people who had handed over the weapons. They did not intend to fight the army and therefore should enjoy the full protection of the bodies of power in -- in the -- in the area. That's what I meant when I said that this should be registered with the heads of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... let me stop you there. Maybe you didn't misunderstand -- maybe you misunderstood earlier. Page 67, Mr. Zecevic was asking you at line 9: "Do you remember the document and you also remember the signature of the late Milorad Kotlica, don't you?" And you said: "Yes, this is his signature." Didn't you just say now that that signature is someone else's?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, if I may be of assistance. I believe the witness was commenting the log-book entry, 192, when -- when he was referring to the handwriting. Not the document that you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that correct, sir? Did I misunderstood you?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The signature in -- on -- in the document is the Colonel's document whereas the log-book was signed by the operative who dispatched the telegram. It may be for that reason that the number was omitted. So the document bears the Colonel's name, whereas the log-book bears the signature of an operative.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. My apology. Let me ask you about -- at page 69, line -- well, line 25. You mentioned that you had a disrupted communication. And then you were talking about the MUP system. "When they came to Pale they had problems with the facility at Kikinda and the facility at Kalovita Brda. They had huge problems. Only very late did they start to function under more or less normal conditions." Because of those difficulties, did they not ask you sometimes to assist them in delivering documents; and did you do that for the MUP in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes, but not often. We always lended a helping hand. Not only to them, but also to the municipality, and to anybody else who wanted our assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And did they return the favour on occasions when they were able to help you?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: For example, when our system of communications was down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, likewise, with the army. Did the army help you and the MUP when it could, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ST-219
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure that they did. There was a level of cooperation between all of us. We had to help each other, in order to be able to protect the population. They helped us when we needed to dispatch certain documents to certain stations. And the MUP used the police stations in the municipalities which could then forward documents that we had not been able to forward to. For example, presidents of municipalities, or socio-political organisations. This was all with a view to creating the most resistant and resilient system of communications because our systems of communications were targeted, and they were down for one reason or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I don't have any further questions for you. I appreciate your coming in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you as well, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, we thank you for your assistance to the Tribunal. Your testimony has been completed within the compass of today's sitting, so you are now released. We thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And I would like to thank you for your fairness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, we are scheduled to resume at 2.15 tomorrow. Would your witness be ready? The witness that you indicated who is coming in, was it this evening?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wasn't clear on when he was coming in but I had understood from Ms. Korner that the witness wouldn't not [sic] be ready to start before Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I do recall this issue of Wednesday in our earlier discussions today. So my -- what I'm really asking is when we -- when we reconvene tomorrow at 2.15 we will be reconvening for the purpose of ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Just to see each other once again. I understand that Ms. Korner maybe had a couple of procedural matters to raise but I don't know if you want to convene for that purpose. I hesitate to say let's not meet tomorrow for fear that there is something that she urgently wants to raise. I don't know what to suggest. I'm trying to contact her at the moment, but I'm not able to have the information from her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, bearing in mind the -- among other things, the transportation of the accused from UNDU to the Tribunal, the... could we -- we be advised before 11.00 tomorrow as to whether it is necessary to meet at 2.15 tomorrow afternoon. And in the absence of such communication, I assume we will -- and I state parenthetically that I suppose everyone would have seen the adjusted schedule that we were due to sit on Wednesday and Thursday in the morning -- that we will take the adjournment to 9.00 Wednesday morning subject to any communication that the Office of the Prosecutor has, as to a need to sit tomorrow afternoon, beginning at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did have a communication that indicated one matter Ms. Korner wanted to be heard on, it concerns a document just disclosed in connection with the next witness to be called. I think she would like to be heard on before he starts on Wednesday and preferably would like to do it tomorrow. But I don't know if it is necessary for the accused to be transported, if that's the only discussion we're going to have. Certainly they're entitled to be. But it might be the kind of thing they're willing or wanting to wait; I don't know. But we'll certainly advise you before 11.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we might as well communicate directly with the Office of the Prosecutor concerning that document and then inform Your Honours on Wednesday morning and -- and whatever submissions needs to be made at that point. The -- I don't see any point that we meet for a document which we might communicate otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm strongly inclined to agree with you Mr. Zecevic. It seems to me an enormous waste of resources to sit tomorrow just to deal with the admission of a document. So unless I'm persuaded otherwise -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we will take the adjournment to Wednesday morning. The -- there is an application in respect of Witness 244 who is scheduled to testify, I believe, next week. So the -- it would be of assistance if we could have expedited responses from the Defence and taking advantage of tomorrow, we would hear from you, no doubt, on Wednesday morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We will, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 24th day of November, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.
